Starting with with work of Michail et al., the problem of
            Counting
            the number of nodes in Anonymous Dynamic Networks has attracted a lot of attention. The problem is challenging because nodes are indistinguishable (they lack identifiers and execute the same program), and the topology may change arbitrarily from round to round of communication, as long as the network is connected in each round. The problem is central in distributed computing, as the number of participants is frequently needed to make important decisions, including termination, agreement, synchronization, among others. A variety of distributed algorithms built on top of
            mass-distribution
            techniques have been presented, analyzed, and experimentally evaluated; some of them assumed additional knowledge of network characteristics, such as bounded degree or given upper bound on the network size. However, the question of whether Counting can be solved deterministically in sub-exponential time remained open. In this work, we answer this question positively by presenting M
            ethodical
            C
            ounting
            , which runs in polynomial time and requires no knowledge of network characteristics. Moreover, we also show how to extend M
            ethodical
            C
            ounting
            to compute the sum of input values and more complex functions without extra cost. Our analysis leverages previous work on random walks in evolving graphs, combined with carefully chosen alarms in the algorithm that control the process and its parameters. To the best of our knowledge, our Counting algorithm and its extensions to other algebraic and Boolean functions are the first that can be implemented in practice with worst-case guarantees.

result.paraphrase: Since the work of Michail et al., the problem of counting the number of nodes in anonymous dynamic networks has drawn considerable attention. It is difficult because the nodes are indistinguishable, with no identifiers and all running the same program, while the topology may change arbitrarily from one communication round to the next, provided the network remains connected in every round. This problem is fundamental in distributed computing, since knowing the number of participants is often necessary for key decisions such as termination, agreement, synchronization, and others. Many distributed algorithms based on mass-distribution techniques have been proposed, analyzed, and tested experimentally; some rely on extra assumptions about network properties, such as bounded degree or a known upper bound on network size. Yet whether counting can be solved deterministically in sub-exponential time was still open. Here we resolve that question affirmatively by introducing Methodical Counting, a polynomial-time algorithm that needs no knowledge of network characteristics. We further show that Methodical Counting can be extended, at no additional cost, to compute the sum of input values and more complex functions. Our analysis builds on earlier results on random walks in evolving graphs, together with carefully designed alarms in the algorithm that regulate the process and its parameters. To our knowledge, our counting algorithm and its extensions to other algebraic and Boolean functions are the first practical implementations with worst-case guarantees.
